In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms involved in the recognition and binding of drugs to DNA.
the structural basis of drug action, and in particular, the interaction between DNA and the intercalating drug daunomycin.
the elucidation of the molecular details of drug-DNA interactions and their relationship to biological effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

daunomycin intercalates in a head-on manner, and is stabilized by hydrogen-bonding to the intercalation site, by van der Waals interactions with the sugar-phosphate backbone, and by electrostatic interactions with the amino sugar N-2' substituent.
daunomycin binds to d(CGATCG), with the chromophore intercalated at right-angles between base-pairs, and the sugar and cyclohexene in the minor groove, in a sequence-dependent manner.

the daunomycin chromophore is intercalated in a head-on fashion, with the amino sugar lying in the minor groove, in a manner that is stabilized by a combination of direct and solvent-mediated hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions with the DNA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the daunomycin-DNA interaction is a combination of electrostatic and van der Waals forces, and that the drug is positioned in a way that allows it to interact simultaneously with two base-pairs.
daunomycin intercalation is a dynamic process involving a range of conformations.
the structure of the daunomycin-d(CGTACG) complex, which was the first DNA-drug complex to be determined by X-ray crystallography, is a reasonable model of the daunmoycin-d(CGATCG) structure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in addition to the direct hydrogen bonding between the drug and DNA base-pairs, the drug is held in place by a complex pattern of van der Waals interactions with the DNA sugar-phosphates.

the daunomycin chromophore intercalates in the DNA helix in a head-on fashion, with the sugar substituent lying in the minor groove and the amino group forming a hydrogen bond to the O-2 of a thymine.
